<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We reinterpret the final Large Language Model (LLM) softmax classifier as an Energy-Based Model (EBM), decomposing the sequence-to-sequence probability chain into multiple interacting EBMs at inference. This principled approach allows us to track “energy spills” during decoding, which we empirically show correlate with factual errors, biases, and failures. Similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>, our method localizes the exact answer token and subsequently tests for hallucinations. Crucially, however, we achieve this without requiring trained probe classifiers or activation ablations. Instead, we introduce two completely training-free metrics derived directly from output logits: <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spilled energy</span>, which captures the discrepancy between energy values across consecutive generation steps that should theoretically match, and <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">marginalized energy</span>, which is measurable at a single step. Evaluated on nine benchmarks across state-of-the-art LLMs (including LLaMA, Mistral, and Gemma) and on synthetic algebraic operations (Qwen3), our approach demonstrates robust, competitive hallucination detection and cross-task generalization. Notably, these results hold for both pretrained and instruction-tuned variants without introducing any training overhead. Code available at <a href="http://github.com/OmnAI-Lab/spilled-energy/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">github.com/OmnAI-Lab/spilled-energy/</a></p>
  
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various domains has brought increasing attention
to their critical limitation: their tendency to generate
incorrect or misleading information—commonly referred
to as “hallucinations.” This issue supports the idea
that LLMs are just stochastic parrots <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bender et al., 2021</a>)</cite> answering in a way that is statistically plausible with respect to the input prompt despite not having a real understanding of it.
On the other side, recent reasoning capabilities proper to ChatGPT 4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI-Team, 2023</a>)</cite> or Deepseek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> offer counter evidence to actually support this.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Ongoing research seeks to characterize and categorize hallucinations, setting them apart from other error types <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawte et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. At the same time, recent discussions have introduced terms such as confabulations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Millidge, 2023</a>)</cite> and fabrications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">McGowan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, sometimes attributing a form of “intention” to LLMs—though the very idea of LLM “intentionality” and other human-like qualities remains contested <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salles et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Serapio-García et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Harnad, 2024</a>)</cite>.
Research on LLM hallucinations can be categorized into two main branches: the first one is the extrinsic branch, where the hallucinations are measured with respect to the interpretation that humans give to those errors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawte et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
The second branch was started by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al. (2022b)</a></cite>, proposing to study the hallucinations <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">within</em> the model itself. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al. (2022b)</a></cite>, the work in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2024)</a></cite> proposes Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) as a way to improve the “truthfulness” of LLMs at inference time.
ITI functions by altering model activations at inference time, steering them along specific directions within a restricted set of attention heads.
Our work is also different from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2023)</a></cite>, since we care about detecting errors in LLMs, whereas they introduce an automated methodology to detect when LLMs are aware that they do not know how to answer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we follow the definition of hallucinations given by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite> as any form of error produced by an LLM—including factual mistakes, biased outputs, breakdowns in common-sense reasoning, and related issues.
Like them, we also confirm that the truthfulness signal is concentrated in the “exact answer tokens.” Nevertheless, unlike them, we abandon the idea of using a probe classifier <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belinkov, 2022</a>)</cite> trained for each task and dataset. Given that LLMs are foundational models, user interactions typically occur <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in the wild</em>, making it difficult to predict which probe classifier is best suited for detecting hallucinations in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, in this setting, classifier weights should not only be updated dynamically for each task, but the optimal token–layer combination is also dataset-dependent, which conflicts with the broad LLM applicability.
Indeed, in the work by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>, the authors report:</p>
<blockquote id="S1.p3.2" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="S1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">“We find that probing classifiers do not generalize across different tasks.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p id="S1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">In our paper, we propose to solve this problem with a training-free method that generalizes better across different tasks and is mathematically principled using the framework of Energy-based Models (EBMs). <a href="#S0.F1" title="In Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports a qualitative comparison across tasks, comparing to the logit confidence. Additional samples are shown in <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We reinterpret the final softmax classifier over the vocabulary of LLM as an EBM, taking inspiration from what <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grathwohl et al. (2020)</a></cite> did for classifiers.
This perspective enables us to decompose the sequence-to-sequence probability chain into multiple interacting EBMs that operate jointly during inference. Through this decomposition, we introduce the notion of “spilled energy” in LLM decoding and show empirically that such spill strongly correlates with errors. Given that our method is solely based on the mathematics of EBMs and the chain rule of probability, we do not have to train or tune our detector, striking a good generalization across tasks and LLMs.
Building on this foundation, our contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training-free, LLM hallucination detection generalizing across tasks using the EBM framework. We introduce a method for detecting hallucinations that requires no additional training, in contrast to prior work that relies on trained classifiers and ablations of model activations. Our approach directly reads values inside the LLM, enabling natural generalization across tasks and performing better than logit-based detection.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Two energy-based metrics. We define two complementary measures of energy spills: (i) delta energy <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>, which captures discrepancies between energy values across two time steps that should be mathematically equivalent, and (ii) marginal energy <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>, which can be evaluated at a single time step.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scalable and generalizable analysis. Our framework is mathematically principled, training-free, and exhibits strong cross-dataset generalization. We scale our analysis to state-of-the-art LLMs, including Llama 3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, and demonstrate competitive performance across nine benchmarks, showing robustness across datasets and architectures.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a) illustrates the core idea of our method: rather than using a naïve approach, such as simply recording the logit or training a probe classifier at the activations of the answer token, we first reinterpret the LLM as an autoregressive EBM via the chain rule of probabilities. We then further decompose each conditional probability, incorporating insights from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grathwohl et al. (2020)</a></cite>. At the time step of the exact token <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i-1</annotation></semantics></math>, we extract the energy, which corresponds to the logit, and compare it with the marginal energy at the next time step <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to the denominator of the softmax. According to the chain rule, these two quantities should be identical; however, they differ in the LLM implementation—<a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b).
We find that the discrepancy, which we term spilled energy <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>, correlates strongly with instances where the LLM produces an incorrect output—see <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(c). Moreover, its detection signal separates well correct and incorrect classes across datasets, reflecting the model’s confidence, as shown in <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(d).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18671v1/spilled_idea_5.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/221;" width="494" height="221" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">How energy spills in LLMs</span>. (a) Language Modeling <math id="S1.F2.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math> is attained as a decomposition problem following the chain rule of probability, implemented as autoregressive: we recursively apply a discriminative classifier over the vocabulary <math id="S1.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> to attain generative modeling with larger context size i.e. <math id="S1.F2.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\mathbf{x}_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{x}_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})</annotation></semantics></math>. (b) We reinterpret each discriminative classifier as a generative EBM, finding a connection between two quantities that should be the same across time steps yet are different. We call this difference “the spilled energy” <math id="S1.F2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math> in <a href="#S4.E8" title="In Definition 4.1 (Spilled Energy Δ𝐸_𝜽(𝐱_{𝑖:1})). ‣ 4.1 Interpreting LLMs as Energy-based models (EBMs) ‣ 4 How Energy Spills in LLMs ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. (c) Given that we simply read values inside the LLM, our approach is training-free and correlates well with hallucinations on a synthetic math dataset with increasing difficulty; (d) histograms of spilled energy values, for incorrect and correct answers on all nine datasets using <math id="S1.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>min</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min</annotation></semantics></math> pooling for Llama-3-Instruct. The two distributions are easily separable by using a simple threshold, resulting in a generalization across real-world tasks.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EBM applications to Trustworthy AI.</span> EBMs have been applied to improve the reliability and interpretability of Deep Nets. For example, Energy-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection (OOD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2020</a>)</cite> uses the energy score as a more robust alternative to softmax confidence. At the same time, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grathwohl et al. (2020)</a></cite> presents how to reinterpret a discriminative classifier as EBM to train models that are both discriminative and generative. Following this work, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al. (2021)</a></cite> provides new insights into the role of energy when training EBMs and robust classifiers using adversarial training. Instead, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mirza et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mirza et al. (2025)</a></cite> explain adversarial attacks by reinterpreting the softmax classifier as an EBM, showing that these perturbations correspond to shifts in the underlying energy landscape.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Foundations of Hallucination in LLMs.</span> LLMs are prone to diverse errors—including bias, reasoning failures, and generation of factually incorrect information unsupported by reliable sources. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpowicz (2025)</a></cite> frames hallucination and imagination as mathematically identical phenomena, both emerging from a necessary violation of information conservation. Also <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al. (2025)</a></cite> provides a formal learning-theoretic proof that hallucinations are unavoidable. They define a <span id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">formal world</span> in which both the LLM and the ground-truth are computable functions, showing through classic results in computability theory, that no LLM can learn all such functions. As a consequence, hallucination is not just a practical artifact but a fundamental limitation of LLMs, valid even under idealized conditions.
Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalai et al. (2025)</a></cite> showed that hallucinations come from the statistical problem of the pretraining methodology: minimizing the cross entropy naturally causes errors because it does not train the model to express uncertainty and say “I do not know.” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalai et al. (2025)</a></cite> proposes changing the evaluation practices to not reward models for guessing, but rather to mimic the human exams that penalize only wrong answers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Detecting and Mitigating LLM Hallucinations.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite> train classifiers on the internal representations of the LLMs to predict, based on the features, the correctness of the answer. Given an LLM in a white-box setting, an input prompt, and the generated response <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math>, the classifier’s task is to predict whether <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math> is a hallucination.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al.</a></cite> suggested that LLMs may encode more factual knowledge in their latent subspaces than is revealed in their outputs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gekhman et al. (2025)</a></cite> proposed a framework for studying hidden knowledge. Finally, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Santilli et al. (2025)</a></cite> point out that uncertainty quantification in language models is often evaluated using metrics like AuROC. This shares biases between detection methods and correctness functions (e.g., length effects) that systematically distort results.
One way to mitigate hallucinations is to act at the decoding stage, where the output generation can be steered <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramani et al. (2022)</a></cite>. Steering vectors provide a straightforward way to control a model by adding a fixed vector to its activations  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dunefsky and Cohan, 2025</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduced DeepConf, a test-time method that leverages model-internal confidence signals to filter out low-quality reasoning traces during or after generation.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuhn et al. (2023b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fadeeva et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Farquhar et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and its follow-up by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kossen et al. (2025)</a></cite> in which they approximate the semantic entropy in a more efficient way.
Constrained decoding approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al. (2023)</a></cite> modify token selection policies.
Similarly, reinforcement learning with fact-based rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al. (2022)</a></cite> has been used to bias decoding trajectories toward verifiable outcomes.
Incorrect answers may also be given due to an ambiguous prompt: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuhn et al. (2023a)</a></cite>’s CLAM framework uses few-shot prompts to classify a question’s ambiguity and then asks the user to clarify.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Background and Foundations</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Energy-Based Models</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We give an overview of Energy-based Models (EBMs) and their use in discriminative classifiers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EBMs.</span> Energy-Based Models are a class of probabilistic models in which the probability distribution over data points <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined in terms of an energy function <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math>. The energy function, parameterized by a neural network <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lecun et al., 2006</a>)</cite>, assigns a scalar energy to each configuration of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, where lower energy values correspond to higher likelihood. The resulting probability distribution is given by <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp(-E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}))}{Z_{\bm{\theta}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp(-E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}))}{Z_{\bm{\theta}}}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the partition function (normalizing constant), defined as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{\bm{\theta}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\exp(-E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></msub><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{\bm{\theta}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\exp(-E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}))</annotation></semantics></math> for discrete <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, or equivalently <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{\bm{\theta}}=\int\exp(-E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}))\,d\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{\bm{\theta}}=\int\exp(-E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}))\,d\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> for continuous <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>. Standard neural networks are often deterministic function approximators, mapping <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\mapsto y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\mapsto y</annotation></semantics></math>, EBMs instead define a full probability distribution over data or latent variables.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One of the strengths of EBMs is their flexibility in modeling arbitrary distributions without being tied to a specific parametric form. This flexibility comes from the fact that the energy function <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> can be defined in various ways. Training involves learning the parameters of the energy function such that the probability distribution <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> matches the empirical distribution of the data. This is typically achieved using techniques like contrastive divergence, score matching, or maximum likelihood.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Notation.</span>
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the vocabulary of an LLM, i.e., the set of all tokens that can be processed as input and generated at each decoding step, with size <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{V}|=V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{V}|=V</annotation></semantics></math>.
We shorten the sequence of tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}_{N},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{1}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}_{N},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{1}\}</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{N:1}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{N:1}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the token in the <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th position along the sequence.
We model the LLM as a function
<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>V</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{V}</annotation></semantics></math>,
implemented by a transformer, or any other sequence-to-sequence mechanism.
For a sequence <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}_{i:1}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}_{i:1}\}</annotation></semantics></math> as input, we write <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{\theta}\big(\mathbf{x}_{i:1}\big)[k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}\big(\mathbf{x}_{i:1}\big)[k]</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the predicted logit assigned to the <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th token class in <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> for the <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i+1</annotation></semantics></math> token in the sequence, as is standard in autoregressive LLM training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Autoregressive Large Language Models</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative modeling has been pursued through a variety of approaches beyond autoregression (AR). Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Welling, 2014</a>)</cite> learn a probabilistic latent variable model by encoding inputs into a latent space and decoding samples back to the data domain. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al., 2014</a>)</cite> frame generation as a min-max game between a generator and a discriminator. The diffusion process has been incorporated into neural nets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015</a>)</cite> and, more recently, Diffusion Models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite> have emerged as a powerful class of generative models. While these paradigms differ in how they approximate the data distribution, AR models are special in their kind and take a more direct route by factorizing the joint probability of sequences into conditionals, making them especially suitable for language modeling. We now focus on the AR formulation that underlies most LLMs.
Textual data is segmented into a sequence of tokens <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{1}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{1}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a language modeling objective is employed to maximize the likelihood of such data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford and Narasimhan, 2018</a>)</cite>.
In other words, we model the joint probability of tokens in the sequence <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>, through a conditional probability parameterized by <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})=p(\mathbf{x}_{i}\ |\ \mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})\ldots p(\mathbf{x}_{2}\ |\ \mathbf{x}_{1})\ p(\mathbf{x}_{1})=\prod\limits_{i}\underbrace{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}\ |\ \mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})}_{\text{discriminative model}}\ p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{1})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.667em" rspace="0.500em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munder><mo p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{1}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">What we find interesting about this factorization is that, although it seeks to attain <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generative modeling</em>, i.e., <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>, it actually uses recursively <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">discriminative classifiers</em>, parameterized by a transformer network <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, that predicts a discrete distribution of the next token <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> over the vocabulary <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>, given previous tokens <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is used to model each conditional probability.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>How Energy Spills in LLMs</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When predicting the token at position <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, the conditional probability modeled by <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> can be decomposed using the probabilities of the sequences. As a result, the marginal term from step <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> cancels out with the sequence probability from the decomposition at the previous step <math id="S4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i-1</annotation></semantics></math>, which means we have:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This indeed confirms that <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.2 Autoregressive Large Language Models ‣ 3 Background and Foundations ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> results in the correct formulation for language modeling, which is <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>. Following the mathematics, these quantities should cancel out along the sequence, but we will now show that, in practice, <em id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">this constraint is not explicitly optimized for, and we can exploit it for hallucination detection.</em></p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Interpreting LLMs as Energy-based models (EBMs)</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let us continue the expansion from <a href="#S4.E2" title="In 4 How Energy Spills in LLMs ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Writing the conditional as the ratio between the joint distribution in the numerator and the marginal distribution in the denominator, we note that this ratio is actually implemented in LLMs as a softmax classifier that digests the embedding of the prior sentence <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1}</annotation></semantics></math> and predicts the next token <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>; thus, this chain of equality holds true. We can then apply the “trick” from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grathwohl et al. (2020)</a></cite> as:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})=\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})}{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})}=\frac{\exp{\bm{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})\left[\texttt{id}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right]}}{\sum\limits_{k=1}^{V}\exp{\bm{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})[k]}}\ \text{where}\ \texttt{id}:\ \{0,1\}^{V}\mapsto[1,\ldots,V]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>[</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">id</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>V</mi></msup><mi>exp</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mtext>where</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">id</mtext><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.778em">:</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>V</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})=\frac{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})}{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})}=\frac{\exp{\bm{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})\left[\texttt{id}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right]}}{\sum\limits_{k=1}^{V}\exp{\bm{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})[k]}}\ \text{where}\ \texttt{id}:\ \{0,1\}^{V}\mapsto[1,\ldots,V].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">id</span> is the map that takes as input a one-hot encoding vector <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> for a word token at position <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> in the text and outputs its index in the vocabulary.
A typical cross-entropy loss only optimizes with the supervision provided by the ground-truth token, through the vocabulary index <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{id}(\mathbf{x}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">id</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{id}(\mathbf{x}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>. This loss ignores all other quantities or constraints related to the complete sequence <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., it ignores all the time steps higher than <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i+1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            For a formal proof, please see <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Partition Functions Proof used in ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}},~E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.497em">,</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}},~E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> are computed from the output of the model, but with two big differences: <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> as a single <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">logit</span> extracted using the <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">id</span> of the sampled token, <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> by <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">marginalizing</span> over all <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ids</span> in the vocabulary.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<p id="S4.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1})</annotation></semantics></math> produces the logits over the entire vocabulary <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{id}(\mathbf{x}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">id</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{id}(\mathbf{x}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> allows us to extract the logit of the sampled token at decoding step <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We can think of <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" <span id="S4.Thmdefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmdefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 4.1</span></span><span id="S4.Thmdefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Spilled Energy <math id="S4.Thmdefinition1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">E</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">𝐱</mi><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">i</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0.278em" mathcolor="#000000" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">1</mn></mrow></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>)<span id="S4.Thmdefinition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<span id="S4.Thmdefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.Thmdefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmdefinition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The spilled energy in an LLM is the difference between two energies that, in principle, should be equal, but given that they are measured i) at different time steps ii) in different components, could be different.</span></span>
<span id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Since both terms on the right side should be equal to <math id="S4.SS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>, delta values should always be zero when we are correctly modeling the energy at timestep <math id="S4.SS1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>. A shorter explanation for why spilled energy needs to be zero is given in <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Why Spilled Energy should be zero? ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Detecting hallucinations with spilled energy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EBMs have previously been used to assess neural network credibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and calibration for LLMs has been explored by the Anthropic team <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>.
However, dominant training-free baselines such as logits or “<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\text{true})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>true</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\text{true})</annotation></semantics></math>” remain weak.
We likewise adopt a training-free approach, but rely on <a href="#S4.E8" title="In Definition 4.1 (Spilled Energy Δ𝐸_𝜽(𝐱_{𝑖:1})). ‣ 4.1 Interpreting LLMs as Energy-based models (EBMs) ‣ 4 How Energy Spills in LLMs ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and its variants as discriminants.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We feed the prompt <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}_{i-1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{1}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}_{i-1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{1}\}</annotation></semantics></math> to the LLM <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and obtain the completion <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}_{N},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{i}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}_{N},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{i}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we focus on the “exact answer” tokens—those in <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[i+1,N]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[i+1,N]</annotation></semantics></math> that contain the precise answer (e.g., <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Rome</span> in <a href="#S0.F1" title="In Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), denoted <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[u,w]\subseteq[i+1,N]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊆</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[u,w]\subseteq[i+1,N]</annotation></semantics></math>. For instance, it would be the tokens associated with <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Rome</span> in the question in <a href="#S0.F1" title="In Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
We identify this span by prompting the LLM for a brief answer.
When the answer spans multiple tokens, we apply a pooling strategy, which we ablate in <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
We propose measuring two values that correlate well with hallucinations:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Marginal energy <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Spilled energy <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math> by definition of <a href="#S4.E8" title="In Definition 4.1 (Spilled Energy Δ𝐸_𝜽(𝐱_{𝑖:1})). ‣ 4.1 Interpreting LLMs as Energy-based models (EBMs) ‣ 4 How Energy Spills in LLMs ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We also attempt to combine the two metrics into scaled spilled energy <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta E_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the spilled energy is multiplied by the absolute value of the marginal energy as
<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta E_{s}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})=\lvert E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})\rvert\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{s}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})=\lvert E^{m}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})\rvert\Delta E_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The metrics proposed here are independent, new for LLMs, and can all be tested efficiently. These measures can be computed over the full sequence, but for error detection, as discussed in <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, we must extract the values in the localized exact interval <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[u,w]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[u,w]</annotation></semantics></math> to avoid false positives. Note that <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>𝜽</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\ell}_{\bm{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i:1})</annotation></semantics></math> is the classic baseline which in literature is referred to as “logits” or “logits confidence”.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate spilled energy, we consider two complementary settings.
First, a controlled synthetic environment, where we generate both correct and incorrect multi-digit arithmetic solutions. Second, established real-world benchmarks, where errors arise naturally across diverse reasoning and comprehension tasks. Together, these experiments test whether insights from the clean synthetic setup transfer to the complexity of open-domain language understanding.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Setting.</span>
We first evaluate spilled energy in a controlled setting: multi-digit arithmetic problems with more than 14 digits. For each instance, we generate both correct and incorrect solutions. We tested three different LLMs: Llama-3 8B (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al.</a></cite>), Qwen-3 8B (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen-Team</a></cite>), and Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.3 (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al.</a></cite>).
Incorrect solutions are obtained by introducing random numerical errors of varying magnitude.
Specifically, we define three error ranges that differ in their difficulty of detection:</p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S5.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Easy</span>: random offset in the range <math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1000,10000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1000,10000]</annotation></semantics></math>, which are typically easier to identify.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S5.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Medium</span>: random offset in the range <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[100,1000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[100,1000]</annotation></semantics></math>, where detection requires closer inspection.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S5.I1.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hard</span>: random offset in <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,10]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,10]</annotation></semantics></math>, much harder to detect since they appear plausible at first glance.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This design allows us to systematically probe whether spilled energy can distinguish between correct and incorrect generations across different levels of error subtlety.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span>
We observe that spilled energy values separate correct from incorrect solutions with high reliability across all error ranges and across all LLMs.
In particular, spilled energy consistently assigns lower values to correct generations and higher values to incorrect ones, producing a clear margin of separation.
Compared to standard baselines such as <em id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">logits</em>, spilled energy achieves superior discriminative power, especially for errors in the more challenging range <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,10]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,10]</annotation></semantics></math>, see <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We offer more results in <a href="#A4.F5" title="In D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Larger, better-detailed ROC and histograms are in <a href="#A4.F7" title="In D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and <a href="#A4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> respectively.</p>
</div>
