<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Setting.</span>
We evaluate our methods on a diverse set of established NLP benchmarks, including Math (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al.</a></cite>), TriviaQA (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joshi et al.</a></cite>), HotpotQA (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al.</a></cite>), Winogrande (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sakaguchi et al.</a></cite>), Winobias (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al.</a></cite>), Movies (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al.</a></cite>), MNLI (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams et al.</a></cite>) and IMDB (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maas et al.</a></cite>).
These datasets span a wide range of reasoning and error-detection tasks, allowing us to test whether the patterns observed in the synthetic arithmetic setting extend to real-world, open-domain scenarios. Here too, we evaluate multiple LLMs that are either instruction-aligned or not aligned, such as LLaMA-3 (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al.</a></cite>), and Mistral (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al.</a></cite>).
As emphasized by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al.</a></cite>, it is essential to first localize the tokens most relevant to the final answer before applying error detection. Since exact answer tokens may consist of multiple tokens, we further adopt a pooling strategy across the localized span to obtain a final score per sentence.
We compare spilled and marginal energy against baselines such as the probing classifiers of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al.</a></cite>, logit confidence of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Varshney et al.</a></cite> and <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\text{true})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>true</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\text{true})</annotation></semantics></math> of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadavath et al.</a></cite>.</p>
</div>

<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation of the exact answer token.</span> We provide an ablation experiment on the impact of selecting the exact answer tokens. <a href="#S5.T2" title="In 5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports average AuROC over 9 benchmarks and 3 LLMs with the exact answer, along with another column that offers the improvement provided by using the exact answer. Like prior work, we confirm that searching for the exact answer provides a notable boost: the improvement is very pronounced (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 24\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>24</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 24\%</annotation></semantics></math>) for spilled and marginal energy, while the logit baseline receives a modest increase of <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9\%</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-dataset results.</span> We next evaluate in the more general setting of cross-dataset transfer, which better reflects real-world usage.
For methods requiring training, we report the average performance on each dataset when trained separately on each of the other datasets (e.g., performance on IMDB is the average accuracy of classifiers trained on each of the other nine datasets).
<a href="#S5.F4" title="In 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows a confusion matrix of cross-dataset performance, where the rows represent the training dataset and the columns represent the testing dataset, and where red indicates good performance and blue indicates low accuracy. The model tested is LlaMA-3-Instruct.
<a href="#S5.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a> shows that probing classifiers, as soon as they go out-of-distribution from the training dataset, perform only marginally better than random guessing. The sharp drop observed in the off-diagonal elements supports our premise that this standard, in-distribution setup significantly overestimates the utility of trained probes for broad LLM deployment. Meanwhile, <a href="#S5.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a> displays the improvement of Spilled <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E</annotation></semantics></math> over the probing classifier, where a positive red result means improvement of our method. Ours exhibits greater performance across most datasets without requiring training. The generalization is proved with a strong increment over the off-diagonal. Moreover, in some cases, such as TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and Movies, we have improvements <em id="S5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">even on the diagonal</em>. Additional confusion matrices are available in <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Additional results for Cross-testing with Real World Benchmarks ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes results across nine benchmarks. The result reported in each cell is the average of the accuracies of <a href="#S5.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a> within a column.
Spilled energy consistently outperforms <em id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">logit</em> confidence, and substantially surpasses the probing classifiers of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
While this latter performs well when trained and tested on the same dataset, their performance drops sharply under cross-dataset evaluation, as reflected in their higher standard deviations.
By contrast, ours requires no training and generalizes robustly across diverse benchmarks.
We observe that instruction-tuned models tend to amplify the margin by which spilled energy outperforms other methods, whereas on non-aligned Mistral, spilled energy may rank slightly behind marginal energy.
We also compare pooling strategies and find that <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>min</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min</annotation></semantics></math> pooling yields the best overall performance across methods.
<a href="#S5.T3" title="In 5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows our method generalizes to Gemma over different LLM size, 1B and 4B.</p>
</div>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We observe a difference in the behavior in the base models and their instruction-tuned ones. While instruction-tuning generally improves generation quality, it can degrade the calibration of classical confidence metrics, as described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2023a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al. (2025)</a></cite>. For instance, examining the average performance in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the logit baseline <math id="S5.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\theta}^{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>E</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\theta}^{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> decreases from 56.89% to 54.62% for LLaMA-3, indicating that fine-tuning may lead to overconfidence.
In contrast, Spilled Energy (<math id="S5.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta E_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>) consistently benefits from instruction tuning, showing improved detection rates across both LLaMA-3 (68.69% to 73.16%) and Mistral (73.94% to 77.49%).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Variance and Generalization.</span>
A notable observation in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is the higher standard deviation associated with marginal and spilled energy compared to the probing classifiers in the average column. This variance is not a weakness but a reflection of the method’s training-free nature. Since <math id="S5.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta E_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> relies on the intrinsic energy landscape of the LLM, its magnitude and sensitivity are naturally dependent on the specific domain (e.g., the sharp energy peaks in <span id="S5.SS2.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Math</span> and <span id="S5.SS2.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">HotpotQA</span> versus the flatter distributions in <span id="S5.SS2.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Winobias</span> and <span id="S5.SS2.p7.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">IMDB</span>). Probing classifiers, by contrast, have high-variance when cross-testing yet the average of cross-testing results is mostly constant just above random chance (<math id="S5.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 62-64\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>62</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 62-64\%</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations.</span> 
A current limitation of spilled energy is that it sometimes produces false positives on tokens that are not semantically informative, as shown in <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.
We observe this effect most prominently on punctuation tokens (e.g., commas, periods) and on words at the beginning of sentences.
In these cases, the probability mass over the next token is naturally spread across many plausible options, leading to inflated spilled energy values even in otherwise correct generations.
This highlights the importance of accurately identifying the <em id="S5.SS2.p8.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">exact answer tokens</em>, as detection is most reliable when restricted to the parts of the output that carry the semantic content of the answer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We reinterpreted the softmax layer of LLMs as an EBM, which lets us define
<em id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spilled energy</em>: the discrepancy between energy values that should be equal across
consecutive time steps. We show theoretically and empirically that this discrepancy provides a
strong, training-free signal for detecting hallucinations and errors in LLM outputs.
Through synthetic arithmetic experiments, we demonstrate that spilled energy reliably separates
correct from incorrect generations, outperforming baselines such as logits and marginal energy.
Across diverse real-world NLP benchmarks, spilled energy generalizes robustly without requiring
additional classifiers or task-specific training, unlike probing methods that struggle with transfer.
Overall, spilled energy offers a principled and practical framework for error detection in LLMs and
a new perspective on the internal energy dynamics of autoregressive models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Ethics Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work adheres to the ICLR Code of Ethics.
Our study focuses on methodological contributions to error and hallucination detection in Large Language Models.
We do not train new models or collect additional data; instead, we rely exclusively on publicly available datasets and widely used benchmark models for evaluation.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We note that part of our evaluation includes the Math dataset, which was publicly accessible at the time of experimentation but has since been taken down following a copyright claim.
We emphasize that this dataset was used solely for evaluation purposes of our method, and only prior to the date of the takedown.
No redistribution of the dataset was made, and our reported results are limited to demonstrating methodological effectiveness.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our work does not involve personally identifiable information, sensitive content, or human subjects, and does not raise foreseeable risks of harm.
We believe the proposed approach contributes positively to research on trustworthy AI by providing a training-free and generalizable framework for error detection in language models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Reproducibility Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We are committed to ensuring the reproducibility of our results.
All experimental details, including model configurations, evaluation protocols, and datasets used, are described in the main text and <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Reproducibility ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.
Upon acceptance of this work, we will publicly release the code implementing our method, along with instructions to reproduce all reported experiments.
This will allow the community to verify our findings and build upon our work.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">

<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend the proof of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al.</a></cite> to the sequence-to-sequence setting by treating next-token prediction as a multi-class classification problem.
At step <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, the input is the prefix <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}_{i-1:1}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the model outputs logits over the vocabulary <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> of size <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>.

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, for <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> the model degenerates into a uniform random classifier over the vocabulary.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Interpretation.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Varying <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> perturbs the balance between the two energy terms, introducing a systematic error in <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta E_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>.
From the perspective of the Boltzmann distribution, scaling by <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tfrac{1}{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>τ</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tfrac{1}{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to injecting or removing energy from the system.
At high temperatures (<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>), the system approaches maximum entropy, where all tokens have equal probability.
At low temperatures (<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>), the distribution collapses onto the maximum logit token, making the model highly deterministic.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Error accumulation.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As we generate tokens sequentially, we accumulate deviations in <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta E_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta E_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A1.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E22"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Hence, temperature scaling not only modifies the probabilities but also reshapes the cumulative error landscape traced by spilled energy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Why Spilled Energy should be zero?</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TL;DR</span> Consider Eq. (2) in our paper and the simplification that occurs between the two probabilities between step <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and step <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i-1</annotation></semantics></math>: that simplification occurs because the probability in the denominator at step <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is the same as the probability in the numerator at step <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i-1</annotation></semantics></math> in order to perform language modeling correctly. We measure those inside and LLMs in terms of energy, and the spilled energy is the amount by which they differ.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Please see the definition below. Let us assume a sequence of three tokens <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. If we do language modeling with autoregression, minimizing the negative log-likelihood, we have:</p>

<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">the numerator <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> as the energy <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{2},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math>, which is the <span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">logit (<math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>)</span> of the softmax at timestep 2;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A1.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The denominator as the energy <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{m}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{m}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> obtained with the <span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">marginalization (m)</span> across the vocabulary <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>. This value can be read “read” simply by taking the denominator of the softmax at timestep 2. Please remember this term.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">It is better to indicate them as energies (since they are not probabilities), and given their logarithmic properties, we obtain a difference. We use the notation <math id="A1.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> for logits and <math id="A1.SS3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> for marginalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Now, <span id="A1.SS3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">when we go across steps and we connect two-time steps:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A1.SS3.p9.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\text{{step 1:}}\quad-\log p(\mathbf{x}_{1}|\mathbf{x}_{0})=-\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{0})}=E^{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})-E^{m}(\mathbf{x}_{0})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">step 1:</mtext><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>E</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{{step 1:}}\quad-\log p(\mathbf{x}_{1}|\mathbf{x}_{0})=-\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})}{p(\mathbf{x}_{0})}=E^{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})-E^{m}(\mathbf{x}_{0}).</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">We see that at timestep 1, the value <math id="A1.SS3.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="A1.SS3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">appears again, but measured at the logit level.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p11.1" class="ltx_p">In other words, across the time-steps 2 and 1, the quantity <math id="A1.SS3.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> is measured twice:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p12" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A1.I2.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">at timestep 2, as the marginalization;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A1.I2.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">at timestep 1, as the logit.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p13" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p13.1" class="ltx_p">In the architecture or in the loss, there is no mechanism that forces these quantities to be the same, but they should be equal, given the language modeling objective. This is the same as saying that in <a href="#S4.E2" title="In 4 How Energy Spills in LLMs ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the probabilities across time steps need to cancel out as shown.</p>
</div>

<p id="A1.SS3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">In other words, the following:</p>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Reproducibility</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For comparisons on real-world tasks, we adopt the same experimental setting as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>, whose implementation is publicly available at <a href="https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/LLMsKnow" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/LLMsKnow</a>.
This ensures that our baselines and evaluation procedures follow an established and validated protocol.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, we release our codebase, which includes:</p>
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A2.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">computation of the proposed energy-based measures;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A2.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">scripts for reproducing the synthetic arithmetic preliminary experiments;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A2.I1.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">example of how our method can be integrated into a benchmarking or production pipeline.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Exact Answer Token Detection Details</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To analyze the <span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spilled energy</span> specifically on the tokens carrying the semantic weight of the answer, we must first localize the ”exact answer” span <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[u,w]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[u,w]</annotation></semantics></math> within the longer generated sequence <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math>. We adopt the methodology proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>, utilizing a combination of heuristics and an auxiliary instruction-tuned LLM to perform this extraction.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extraction Strategy</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Depending on the nature of the task, we employ two strategies to identify the exact answer substring <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<ul id="A2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A2.I2.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heuristic Matching:</span> For tasks with a closed set of possible labels (e.g., classification tasks or multiple-choice QA), we perform string matching to locate the label within the generation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A2.I2.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-based Extraction:</span> For open-ended generation tasks (e.g., TriviaQA, Math), where the answer form varies, we employ an instruction-tuned model (Mistral-7B-Instruct) to extract the short answer from the long-form generation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompting for Extraction</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we prompt the auxiliary model with the original question <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> and the generated long answer <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math> using the following template:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="255.19" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 255.19" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,255.19) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#B3B3B3;" fill="#B3B3B3" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 8.57 L 0 246.63 C 0 251.36 3.84 255.19 8.57 255.19 L 541.43 255.19 C 546.16 255.19 550 251.36 550 246.63 L 550 8.57 C 550 3.84 546.16 0 541.43 0 L 8.57 0 C 3.84 0 0 3.84 0 8.57 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 8.57 L 0.69 233.64 L 549.31 233.64 L 549.31 8.57 C 549.31 4.22 545.78 0.69 541.43 0.69 L 8.57 0.69 C 4.22 0.69 0.69 4.22 0.69 8.57 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 20.38 240.96)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.8em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="509.21"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Extract from the following long answer the short answer, only the relevant tokens. If the long answer does not answer the question, output NO ANSWER.<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">

<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Verification and Token Mapping</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure robustness, we verify that the extracted string <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is a valid substring of the original generation <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math>. If the extraction is invalid or the model outputs ”<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">NO ANSWER</span>,” we retry the extraction up to five times. If a valid substring is still not found, the sample is excluded from the analysis to avoid identifying incorrect tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Once the substring <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is validated, we map it to the corresponding token indices <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[u,w]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[u,w]</annotation></semantics></math> in the original sequence. The spilled energy analysis is then performed specifically over this interval, or pooled across it (e.g., via min-pooling) as described in <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Cross-dataset Results in Real-World Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Answer Extraction Performance</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For answer localization, we achieve accuracy comparable to the results of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite>. We report in <a href="#A2.T4" title="In Verification and Token Mapping ‣ B.1 Exact Answer Token Detection Details ‣ Appendix B Reproducibility ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> the extraction success rate across the full datasets using Mistral-7B-Instruct. Note that some datasets have been excluded (e.g., IMDB, Winobias, Winogrande) since they have a finite set of possible answers that can be used to easily locate the exact answer within the model’s generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Supplementary Material</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This supplementary material is intended to complement the main paper by providing further motivation for our assumptions and design choices, as well as additional ablation studies or plots, such as ROCs and histograms, that could not fit in the main paper.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Additional results for Synthetic Arithmetic</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A4.F5" title="In D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> we augmented <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> in the main paper, also adding the results for <span id="A4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.3</span> and <span id="A4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLaMa-3-8B</span>. The same findings of the figure in the paper also translate to this LLM, meaning that our method generalizes across LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.F6" title="In D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and <a href="#A4.F7" title="In D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> also extend and provide more details of <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> in the main paper by showing, respectively, the histograms and the ROC at a better resolution and displayed in different frames. Also, we have added results for Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.3 and LLaMa-3-8B.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Additional Qualitative Results</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we offer additional results of the detection performance following what is shown in <a href="#S0.F1" title="In Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. We report both success cases and failure cases. While it is difficult to draw conclusions and predict when, why, and on which topics spilled energy may work or not, we noticed that it appears to perform reliably on knowledge-based factual content but, at times, exhibits difficulties with reasoning tasks and numerical information, despite working well on math questions, as demonstrated in <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Spilled Energy under Synthetic Arithmetic ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>. Further investigation is required to better understand and validate these patterns.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Additional results for Cross-testing with Real World Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.T5" title="In D.2 Additional Qualitative Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows how our method compares with the baseline methods, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orgad et al. (2025)</a></cite> and Logit <math id="A4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. This table was obtained by using various pooling methods in the pooling window from which we measure possible hallucinations. More details below based on the example in <a href="#A4.F11" title="In D.3 Additional results for Cross-testing with Real World Benchmarks ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Material ‣ Spilled Energy in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>:</p>
<ul id="A4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A4.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Min</span>: minimum energy value in the pooling window. Energy Measured: <math id="A4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-3</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="A4.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\diamond" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋄</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\diamond</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="A4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
